paragraphs.heading: A force from turning
paragraphs.text: The Coriolis force is a pseudo-force: it appears when you describe motion from inside a frame of reference that rotates relative to an inertial one, meaning a frame that is not accelerating. If the frame turns clockwise, the force pushes to the left of a moving object; if it turns anticlockwise, it pushes to the right. The sideways bending it produces is called the Coriolis effect. When people use that phrase in everyday talk, the rotating frame they mean is nearly always the Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters on Earth
paragraphs.text: Because Earth spins, something moving across its surface traces a curved path rather than a straight line relative to the ground. Earth turns once each sidereal day, so for everyday objects the force cannot be noticed. It shows up only over large distances and long times, as in big movements of air and ocean water, or where great precision counts, as with artillery and missiles. The resulting bending, clockwise north of the equator and counterclockwise south of it, strongly shapes the large-scale patterns of winds and ocean currents.

paragraphs.heading: Right in the north, left in the south
paragraphs.text: Since these motions are held to Earth's surface, usually only the horizontal part of the force matters. North of the equator it turns moving objects to the right of the way they are heading; south of the equator it turns them to the left. The deflection is strongest near the poles, where the local rate of spin around a vertical axis is greatest, and it falls to zero at the equator. So winds and currents do not run straight from high pressure to low pressure, as they would without rotation; they veer off to one side. This effect is what sets cyclones spinning and so lets them form.

paragraphs.heading: How the physics works
paragraphs.text: Newton's laws of motion describe objects in an inertial frame. When those laws are rewritten for a rotating frame, two extra accelerations appear: the Coriolis and the centrifugal. The Coriolis force grows with the rotation rate and with the object's speed within the rotating frame, and it points at right angles both to the frame's spin and to the object's velocity. Such extra forces are called fictitious or pseudo forces, and adding them lets Newton's laws work in the rotating system as if it were inertial. In a frame that does not rotate, they vanish.

paragraphs.heading: An argument about a moving Earth
paragraphs.text: In 1651, Giovanni Battista Riccioli and his assistant Francesco Maria Grimaldi wrote that Earth's rotation should push a cannonball fired northward off to the east. In 1674, Claude François Milliet Dechales described a similar deflection for falling bodies and for projectiles aimed at a pole. All three used it to argue against Copernicus's Sun-centred system: if Earth turned, the effect should appear, and failing to see it meant Earth stood still. Their reasoning was correct, but the effect is so small that nobody measured it until the 19th century.

paragraphs.heading: How it got its name
paragraphs.text: Euler worked out the equation for the Coriolis acceleration in 1749, and Laplace included the effect in his tidal equations in 1778. Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis wrote an 1835 paper on the energy output of machines with rotating parts, such as water wheels, which examined the extra forces seen in a rotating frame. He called this one the "compound centrifugal force". Meteorologists began using the term Coriolis force early in the 20th century, and by 1920 that was its name. Back in 1856, William Ferrel had already proposed a mid-latitude circulation cell in which this deflection creates the prevailing westerly winds.
